newsitem.title: UK: Russia armed forces deterioration seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: Russia armed forces deterioration seen continuing.

text.p: Russia's under-funded and demoralised armed forces will continue to deteriorate in 1997, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said on Wednesday in a report on the state of the world's military. "The decline in capability in all departments of the Russian armed forces seems set to continue," the IISS said.
The former Soviet armed forces swallowed huge amounts of the state budget during the Cold War but since the break-up of the Communist superpower, military spending has been slashed.

The IISS report estimated that 1995 military expenditure fell by 15 percent to $82 billion, saying the real decline since 1992 had been 45 percent. But despite this, Russia remained the second largest military spender after the United States.
The disastrous 20-month Chechen war, in which Russian troops have been continually out-thought and out-fought by bands of lightly-armed rebels, shows how far the rot has set in.

"The best the Russian armed forces can now do is contain rebel military action, in particular to try to retain control of the larger population centres and the seat of government in the province, until a longer-term political solution is found," the report said.

"Unless the Russian military can improve its joint force operations and engage the rebels in direct hand-to-hand combat, it will be hard-pressed to achieve even that modest objective." The IISS was not impressed by Russian plans to adopt a new military doctrine which calls for the creation of mobile rapid reaction forces to replace the huge World War Two-era monolithic armed formations so favoured in Soviet times. "Organisational changes to develop more mobile formations suitable for operations both within Russia and outside have not been put into effect," said the report.

"While the Russian army can produce well-trained specialised units for particular tasks, it appears that for large-scale, combined-scale operations the standard of training and the maintenance of weapons falls short of that necessary for highly mobile operations requiring flexibility and rapid manoeuvre," the IISS said.

It also doubted President Boris Yeltsin's promise to end conscription by the year 2000, saying the system of employing full-time professional soldiers on contracts was proving very expensive and not attracting the right kind of people.

"Although at present less than half those required to report for military service are doing so, there seems little prospect of maintaining the armed forces' manpower by any other means in the near future," the report said.
Lack of spending meant large parts of the air force were in a lamentable state, it said.

"In some combat units, aircrew have been grounded because of a lack of available flying hours, whereas others are reportedly limited to 30 hours flying a year -- not enough to assure basic flying safety, let alone an effective combat capability."
